zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical cross-check, consulted after independent scan reading: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, page subset supplied in this package; CC BY 4.0. https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ . This is a lexical aid, not authority for this copy’s glyphs or layout.

lines.note: Mayemaye means previously or formerly. Preserve the repeated headword and the roman example after italic Vt,; vo- is divided at the physical line ending, with the complete glyphs and hyphen inside the crop.
Completes the example about a person already known to the addressee. The caron in guenzǒninde is visible, and the Portuguese begins “a person whom already”; retain peßoa and the continuation at de.

Completes the long-standing acquaintance explanation. Preserve the scan's fused atendes rather than modernizing its word separation, and retain the long s in viſto; the final full stop closes this example.

The Japanese expression describes someone known or patronized from long before. Retain the printed votono monogia and the capital I in Portuguese Ia; its explanation continues below, and the flush-left example is not reindented.

Completes the Portuguese statement that the person has long known and favoured the speaker. The scan supports fauorece with u and the final full stop; preserve this as an indented physical continuation.
Mayen is glossed simply as a demon. The short roman headword and italic Portuguese noun are legible; retain the ye spelling rather than replacing it with a modern reading.
The entry names the front part or bow of a saddle and recommends the form Mayetçuua. Preserve the distinct roman preferred form, the cedillas in both languages, and the grave-accented Latin label.

The scan reads ſella, with a visible e omitted by the OCR. Xiriua then introduces the rear part of the saddle; retain the printed fused Aparte and the first de even though another de begins the next row.
Completes the rear-saddle gloss. The scan genuinely repeats de across the line boundary; retain this apparent compositorial redundancy instead of silently deleting the word.

Cadouo touoru explains passing someone's gate. A fresh native enlargement after the NINJAL lexical check confirms the angular v in Mayevatari rather than the OCR's u. Preserve the upright P. label, the roman Japanese synonym, and the isolated Portuguese article O at the right end.
Completes “passing by someone's gate.” The scan supports ß in paßar and the historical contracted spelling polla; retain the separate continuation and terminal full stop.

The compound means the animal's forequarters. Preserve the visible separation between Maye and yeda, and keep the Portuguese definition italic; this is distinct from the feet entry on the preceding page.
Contrasts the hindquarters with the preceding forequarters. Retain initial V, the separated yeda, the paragraph mark, and Portuguese traſeiros with long s; this example remains indented.

The noun is error or delusion, with examples of illuminating or clarifying it. The alternative marker and divided aqi- are visible; retain the physical break and the roman Japanese examples after the italic gloss.

Completes aqiramuru and explains enlightening those who are astray. The tilde is printed over the final o in andaõ, and the word joins closely to errados; retain the candidate's andaõerrados rather than moving the tilde or modernizing spacing.
The example means guiding those in error. Preserve michibiqu with q and the sentence's continuation after aos; the scan contains the full paragraph mark, text, and right-edge context.

Completes the phrase about those who go astray. Correct the OCR's grave-accented andaò to andaõ: the native mark is a nasal tilde over o, matching the preceding example while retaining this row's visible word separation.
The verb means to err or wander, followed by an example of wandering about. Both marks over o point upward and are circumflexes, not carons; preserve ô/ôta and the printed ariqu.
Explains wandering without knowing the way. Ya- begins Yama in the next example; retain the physical hyphen and the switch from italic Portuguese back to roman Japanese.

Completes Yama fucacu vaqe mayô, describing going astray deep in the mountains. Preserve the circumflex in mayô and the nasal abbreviation Rõper; the scan ends with bare ma, without a visible hyphen to add.

runs.text: tos eſpeßos errado ſem ſaber caminho.

lines.note: Completes ma-tos and the explanation of wandering through dense woods without knowing the path. Preserve eſpeßos with long s followed by ß, and keep the physical word division unregularized.

Mayori and Magaſumi denote matter or rheum in the eye. The alternative marker and long s are visible; the final mark after olho is comma-shaped, so retain it as a comma rather than the provisional full stop.
The causative means making someone err or become confused. Retain the historical ſuru/eta principal parts; Sa- begins the sake example continued below and must not be joined across the physical line.

Completes Saqeuo ſuſumete, urging someone to drink sake, and says their mind was confused. Preserve both long s letters in ſuſumete and the causative mayouaxeta; the Portuguese translation starts with divided Fa-.

runs.text: zẽdo o beber, felo ficar alienado, & fora deſi.

lines.note: Completes Fa-zẽdo and says that making him drink left him confused and beside himself. Restore the visible nasal mark in zẽdo, read alienado rather than the OCR's allena do, and replace the spurious terminal hyphen with the printed full stop; preserve felo and fused deſi.
This related verb has the same causative sense as Mayouaxe. Preserve the historical ſu/aita forms rather than imposing a modern past-tense pattern; the short italic Idem is complete in the crop.
Mayu means eyebrows; the example begins the action of drawing them together. Retain the two consecutive u letters in Mayuuo, the long s in fiſo-, and the hyphen leading into the next row.
Completes fiſomuru and explains showing a frown or an unpleasant face. The scan has ruim, including the narrow i omitted by the OCR; preserve the printed Mostrar and the long s in roſto.

The frown is attributed to sadness or astonishment. Qiyetno begins the contrasting expression of joy; retain its final bare t before no as printed, not an inserted Japanese vowel, and keep the paragraph division.
Completes the expression of opening or relaxing the brows in joy. Preserve the roman mayuuo firaqu, the Portuguese reflexive Alegrarſe, and the continuation after moſtrar.

runs.text: alegria de pois dalgũa triſteza. S.

lines.note: Finishes the explanation as joy after sadness. Retain the visibly separated de pois, the tilde on u in dalgũa, and the final S. label rather than modernizing them.
Mayugue denotes the hairs of the eyebrows. The gue spelling is visible and distinct from the preceding Mayu; preserve the long s in the Portuguese plural and the independent headword row.
Mayumi names a tree; the Portuguese only says “a tree so called.” Preserve Aruore and aßi, and do not insert a modern botanical identification unsupported by the printed definition.
Names an implement used to paint eyebrows. Retain the cedilla in tçu, the two long-s forms in Portuguese, and the nasal mark in pintão; the description continues below.
Completes the explanation of painting artificially higher eyebrows. Preserve the nasal abbreviation artificioſamẽte and the visible long s letters; the line's terminal full stop is intact.
Mayuzumi is explained as artificially painted eyebrows. The final i of the headword is worn but visible; retain the long s in artificioſas and the hyphen dividing fa-zem across rows.

runs.text: zem com tinta em Iapão acima das naturaes.

lines.note: Completes the description of painted brows placed above the natural ones in Japan. Preserve Iapão, with initial I and tilde on a, and historical naturaes; the line does not introduce another Japanese term.

runs.text: Pelle de humpeixe do mar, que ſerue

lines.note: Mazame denotes the skin of a sea fish used as a material. Preserve the tightly set humpeixe as in the candidate, the double l in Pelle, and the long s in ſerue; the intended use follows below.

runs.text: pera bainhas de Catanas, ou Vaquizaxis.

lines.note: Specifies sheaths for Catanas or Vaquizaxis. Both Japanese-derived weapon names occur inside the Portuguese explanation and are retained in their visible italic setting, with whole-word typeface flags; preserve pera and the printed spellings.
The adverb means first or for the present. Preserve the doubled z, the editorial Adu. abbreviation with u, and the comma separating the two senses.
The reduplicated adverb has the same meaning as Mazzu. Preserve both doubled-z sequences and the two separate italic abbreviations; it is not a repeated OCR copy of the preceding row.
Mazzumotte is another adverb meaning first or for now. Retain the doubled t, the label Adu., and the final por leading into the next physical row.
Completes the “for now” sense and begins an example expressing initial relief. Preserve the unaccented printed ando, the paragraph mark, and ita- before the continuation below.

Completes itaſu and identifies the source with the roman citation label Mon., flagged for whole-word typeface review. The Portuguese begins “first I rejoice and remain”; retain folgo and the language boundary after the citation.
Completes the example with being relieved or at ease. Preserve both long s letters in deſcanſado and the full stop; the complete short row remains inside its crop.
The adjective concerns poverty, followed by the example “a poor person.” Retain the final ij spelling and the repeated word's physical division after Mazzu- rather than joining it across rows.
Completes Mazzuxij fito, “a poor person.” The terminal j and the Japanese fito are clear; preserve the italic Portuguese gloss and the indented physical row.

The two derived forms denote poverty and the adverbial form of being poor. Remove the OCR's phantom l after initial M; the scan has Mazzuxiſa, then Mazzuxǔ with a visible caron, not a nasal tilde. Preserve the final comma-shaped mark and the widely separated, indented pair on one physical row; all glyphs and the lower rule are inside the crop.

Restore the omitted enlarged M to the headword ME, explained by Manaco and Portuguese “eyes.” The M spans two physical rows and is assigned initial=2; retain the smaller E's sloping setting from the candidate. Remove the false continuation indentation and enlarge the crop to include the complete initial; caſu- begins the first example.

Completes Mega caſumu, describing the eyes becoming clouded. Retain the historical Enneuoaremſe and the divided Me- of the next example. Restore the continuation placement, which is additionally displaced by the large initial beside it.

Completes Mega curamu, the eyes growing dark, and starts Namidani. Preserve the long s letters in the Portuguese reflexive verb and both physical word divisions; restore the visible continuation indentation.
Completes the expression of vision obscured by tears. Retain cururu as printed, the nasal abbreviation cõ, and the hyphen in mui-; the Portuguese continuation remains on the next row.
Completes “many tears” and starts a fuller example about falling tears. Preserve the cedilla in Votçuru, the italic Vt, label, and the divided me-; restore the continuation indentation.

Continues the Japanese account: tears darkened the eyes so the road could not be distinguished clearly. Retain the q in mivaqera-, long s in ſadacani, and the complete roman row, including its final hyphen.

Completes the negative form mivaqerarenu and the description of the situation. Qir. is a roman citation label, flagged for whole-word typeface review; the Portuguese translation begins after it, with its printed reflexive spacing preserved.

runs.text: os olhos com choro não diſcernia o caminho bẽ.

lines.note: Finishes the translation: crying obscured the eyes so the road could not be seen clearly. Retain the nasal marks in não and bẽ and long s in diſcernia; restore the continuation indentation and preserve the full row.

runs.text: Ir ſe o lume dos olhos.

lines.note: The expression concerns losing the light of the eyes, or failing sight. The caron over ǒ is clear; preserve the separated Portuguese Ir ſe and restore continuation indentation within the long ME entry.
The expression means directing one's eyes or attention to something. Preserve q in caquru, the unaccented Portuguese Por, and the nasal abbreviation algũa; the definition continues below.

Completes the sense of attending to or favouring someone, then starts the example about closing the eyes. The right-end mark is a hyphen, not the OCR's full stop: return fu- to be continued by ſagu below.
Completes fuſagu, “close the eyes,” then introduces holding the eyes wide open. Preserve the long s and the doubled t in fatte, with the next verb remaining on the following physical row.

runs.text: Ver com os olhos bem abertos, & fi-

lines.note: Completes Meuo fatte miru, looking with eyes wide open and fixed. Preserve the final fi- and the separate italic Portuguese explanation; restore the row's continuation indentation.
Completes fi-tos and introduces waking or opening the eyes from sleep. Retain both long s letters in ſamaſu and the historical Eſpertar rather than modernizing its spelling.

runs.text: os olhos do ſono. ¶ Item, per met.

lines.note: Completes the literal waking sense, then introduces a metaphorical use. Move the final Me out of italics: it is visibly roman and begins the Japanese example below. Preserve its unhyphenated physical separation from uo.
Completes Meuo ſamaſu in the metaphorical sense of being astonished. The Portuguese distinguishes this from awakening; preserve the repeated long s forms and the indented physical continuation.
Meuo tozzuru is another expression for closing the eyes. Preserve doubled z and the two paragraph signs; the final Me- begins a separate expression and retains its visible hyphen.
Completes Meuo vodorocaſu, explained as being astonished. Retain initial vo and long s rather than modernizing the verb; the final Meuo begins the blinking example below.

Completes the expression for blinking repeatedly. Preserve the printed x and long s in xibamecaſu and the historical vowel sequence in Pestenejar; the next Me is unhyphenated at the physical line end.

runs.text: Quebrar os olhos, ou fazer ce-

lines.note: Completes Meuo tçubuſu, damaging the eyes or causing blindness. Preserve the cedilla and long s, and keep ce- divided from gar on the next row; restore the continuation placement.
Completes ce-gar and gives the synonymous expression involving poking or striking the eyes. Both cedillas and the q in tçuqi are visible; preserve the separated verbs and italic Idem.
The expression means appearing before someone or being seen. Retain Memiyeuo and long s in ſuru; the Portuguese alternative continues after ſer, with no text missing from this row.

Completes “seen by someone,” then introduces someone who does not appear. Preserve the candidate's st distinction in visto where the ligature does not warrant normalization, and retain xenu and the final fi-.

runs.text: Homem que não aparece, ou ha dias q̃

lines.note: Completes fito and begins the explanation of a person who has not appeared for some time. Preserve the nasal mark in não and the q̃ abbreviation; the Portuguese clause continues on the following row.

Finishes the description of someone absent from a place, then introduces the literary expression Memo ayani. Preserve the separate roman phrase and the nasal mark in não; its explanation begins on the next row.

runs.text: P. Modo de agradecer, ou alegrarſe com al

lines.note: Explains Memo ayani as an expression of gratitude or pleasure. Retain the locally sloping P. label and the printed unhyphenated al at the line end, rather than repairing the division of algũa.

Completes al-gũa and introduces an expression of showing emotion in the eyes. Preserve the tilde over u, the q-free spelling cadouo, and the cedilla in tatçuru; Mo- begins the Portuguese explanation below.

runs.text: ſtrar ſinal nos olhos cõ ira, tristeza, &c. ¶

lines.note: Completes Mo-ſtrar and mentions visible signs of anger or sadness. Preserve cõ and the candidate's tristeza where the st ligature does not resolve a different encoding; make the final Me wholly roman instead of the OCR's mixed italic M and roman e.

Completes Mecadono aru fito and begins the description of someone who immediately retains what they see. Preserve cadono and the separate Japanese words; the Portuguese relative explanation continues below.

Finishes the good-retention example and begins its opposite, explained below as quickly forgetting what is seen. Several letters in Mega ne are abraded; retain the candidate's compatible spacing and letters without inventing a better Japanese expression. Preserve the final fi-.

runs.text: He homem q̃ logo ſe lhe var-

lines.note: The scan begins tode, completing fi-tode from the preceding row; retain this printed division. The Portuguese says what is seen is quickly swept from memory. Retain q̃, long s, and the division var-re across rows.

runs.text: re, ou eſquece do que ve. ¶

lines.note: Completes var-re and explicitly says the person forgets what they see. Meuo moru then starts an example about marking a board; preserve the roman phrase and the paragraph boundary, with continuation indentation restored.

Explains making ruled lines and begins the example of Go or shogi boards. Preserve the caron in xǒgui, not a circumflex; these roman game names form part of the Japanese example and are not marked as embedded Portuguese terms.
Completes the Japanese example of ruling a board. Retain doubled n in banni and the historical Portuguese taboleiro; the object of do continues below.

Completes the board explanation, with italic Go embedded in Portuguese and flagged for typeface review. Read the following verb as ſugamuru, not OCR ſugaiuru: the scan shows the joined strokes of m, and the next gloss describes squinting. Lexical comparator: Shogakukan's dictionary entries for 眇む/眇める, reproduced at https://kotobank.jp/word/眇める-540857; consulted only after the native reading.

runs.text: Ver fechando hum pouco os olhos. ¶

lines.note: Explains seeing while partly closing the eyes, confirming the preceding squinting expression. Fito- begins the next Japanese example; preserve the hyphen, hum, and the paragraph division.

Completes Fitomeuo xiranu, with fabacaranu as an alternative, about disregarding others' eyes or social restraint. Preserve the printed x and f spellings and the alternative marker; the Portuguese explanation continues below.
Finishes the lack-of-shame explanation and introduces making the eyes fierce or glaring. Preserve pejo, the roman icaracaſu with long s, and the paragraph boundary within the indented row.

Retain the scan's unusual Remeſmelar: the exact historical Portuguese verb sense is less secure than its visible letters, while the preceding Japanese concerns a fierce look. Meni cacaru then introduces weighing and appearing; preserve the bare Pe at the line end without inventing a hyphen. The lexical caveat is nonblocking.

runs.text: ſarſe em balança. Item, Aparecer, ou ſer

lines.note: Completes Pe-ſarſe, being weighed on a balance, then adds appearing or being seen as another sense. Preserve the two long s letters, the cedilla in balança, and capital Item and Aparecer; the row remains an indented continuation.

Completes the “being seen” sense and introduces something catching the eye. Preserve visto's existing st encoding, the cedilla in tatçu, and the final hyphen in al- before the Portuguese continuation.

runs.text: gũa couſa nos olhos, ou notarſe. ¶

lines.note: Completes al-gũa and explains something being noticed. Correct Vǒme- to Võme-: native enlargement shows a short wavy nasal mark, not the V-shaped caron used elsewhere on this page, consistent with the honorific prefix. Preserve the physical hyphen and all nasal marks.

Completes Võmeni caquru, showing something to an honoured person. Preserve q in caquru, long s in Moſtrar, and ß in peßoa; the definition explains the honorific context without expanding the printed Japanese prefix.

The expression means directing or distributing one's gaze over different places. Preserve the printed cubaru and the unfinished Portuguese por at the end of the page. The word diuerſas below is a catchword, not another body row, and is restored separately from the signature furniture.
